edges.effect_quant: In Framingham, plasma vitamin B12 below 258 pmol/L with high folate predicted roughly a 1-point-per-year faster MMSE decline, but other well-nourished cohorts found little or no association.
edges.mechanism: Low vitamin B12 can raise methylmalonic acid and impair one-carbon metabolism, myelin maintenance, and neuronal energy handling. Those pathways make slower processing and steeper cognitive decline plausible, especially when deficiency is metabolically confirmed rather than inferred from serum B12 alone.
edges.summary: Older-adult cohort studies suggest that low or low-normal B12 status can track with faster cognitive decline, particularly when accompanied by metabolic evidence of deficiency or high folate exposure. The literature is not fully uniform, though, because some healthier cohorts with better baseline nutrition show little association.
edges.caveats: Serum B12 alone may miss functionally important deficiency, and reverse causation or nutritional confounding can blur observational findings. This edge is best interpreted as a plausible risk signal rather than a settled large effect across all elderly populations.

evidence.notes: Biochemical indicators of vitamin B12 and folate insufficiency and cognitive decline.

evidence.citation: Morris MS et al 2012 J Am Geriatr Soc
evidence.notes: Vitamin B-12 and folate status in relation to decline in scores on the mini-mental state examination in the framingham heart study.
Prospective study of plasma folate, vitamin B12, and cognitive function and decline.
